In [[enumerative geometry]], '''Steiner's conic problem''' is the problem of finding the number of smooth [[Conic section|conics]] tangent to five given conics in the plane [[General position|in general position]]. If the problem is considered in the [[complex projective plane]] '''CP'''<sup>2</sup>, the correct solution is 3264.<ref>{{citation |last1=Bashelor |first1=Andrew |title=Enumerative algebraic geometry of conics |journal=Amer. Math. Monthly |volume=115 |number=8 |pages=701–728 |year=2008 |url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/upload_library/22/Ford/Bashelor.pdf |doi=10.1080/00029890.2008.11920584 |jstor=27642583 |mr=2456094 |last2=Ksir |first2=Amy |last3=Traves |first3=Will}}</ref> The problem is named after [[Jakob Steiner]] who first posed it and who gave an incorrect solution in 1848.<ref>{{citation |first=David |last=Eisenbud |author-link=David Eisenbud |last2=Harris |first2=Joe |author-link2=Joe Harris (mathematician) |title=3264 and All That: A Second Course in Algebraic Geometry |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2016 |isbn=978-1107602724|page=290}}</ref>

==History==
Steiner claimed that the number of conics tangent to 5 given conics in general position is 7776&nbsp;=&nbsp;6<sup>5</sup>, but later realized this was wrong.<ref>{{citation |last=Steiner |first=J. |title=Elementare Lösung einer geometrischen Aufgabe, und über einige damit in Beziehung stehende Eigenschaften der Kegelschnitte |journal=J. Reine Angew. Math. |volume=37 |pages=161–192 |year=1848 |url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?PPN243919689_0037}}</ref> The correct number 3264 was found in about 1859 by [[Ernest de Jonquières]] who did not publish because of Steiner's reputation, and by Chasles using his theory of characteristics,<ref>{{citation |last=Chasles |first=M. |title=Construction des coniques qui satisfont à cinque conditions |journal=C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris |volume=58 |pages=297–308 |year=1864}}</ref> and by Berner in 1865. However these results, like many others in classical [[intersection theory]], do not seem to have been given complete proofs until the work of [[William Fulton (mathematician)|Fulton]] and [[Robert MacPherson (mathematician)|MacPherson]] in about 1978.{{sfnp|Eisenbud|Harris|2016|page=292}}

==Formulation and solution==

The space of (possibly degenerate) conics in the complex projective plane '''CP'''<sup>2</sup> can be identified with the [[complex projective space]] '''CP'''<sup>5</sup> (since each conic is defined by a homogeneous degree-2 polynomial in three variables, with 6 complex coefficients, and multiplying such a polynomial by a non-zero [[complex number]] does not change the conic). Steiner observed that the conics tangent to a given conic form a degree 6 [[hypersurface]] in '''CP'''<sup>5</sup>. So the conics tangent to 5 given conics correspond to the intersection points of 5 degree 6 hypersurfaces, and by [[Bézout's theorem]] the number of intersection points of 5 generic degree 6 hypersurfaces is 6<sup>5</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;7776, which was Steiner's incorrect solution. The reason this is wrong is that the five degree 6 hypersurfaces are not in general position and have a common intersection in the [[Veronese surface]], corresponding to the set of double lines in the plane, all of which have double intersection points with the 5 conics. In particular the intersection of these 5 hypersurfaces is not even 0-dimensional but has a 2-dimensional component. So to find the correct answer, one has to somehow eliminate the plane of spurious degenerate conics from this calculation.{{sfnp|Eisenbud|Harris|2016|page=291}}

One way of eliminating the degenerate conics is to [[blowing up|blow up]] '''CP'''<sup>5</sup> along the Veronese surface.{{sfnp|Eisenbud|Harris|2016|pages=291–292}} The [[Chow ring]] of the blowup is generated by ''H'' and ''E'', where ''H'' is the total transform of a [[hyperplane]] and ''E'' is the [[exceptional divisor]]. The total transform of a degree 6 hypersurface is 6''H'', and Steiner calculated (6''H'')<sup>5</sup> = 6<sup>5</sup>''P'' as ''H''<sup>5</sup>=''P'' (where ''P'' is the class of a point in the Chow ring). However the number of conics is not (6''H'')<sup>5</sup> but (6''H''−2''E'')<sup>5</sup> because the strict transform of the hypersurface of conics tangent to a given conic is 6''H''−2''E''.

Suppose that ''L'' = 2''H''−''E'' is the strict transform of the conics tangent to a given line. Then the intersection numbers of ''H'' and ''L'' are given by ''H''<sup>5</sup>=1''P'', ''H''<sup>4</sup>''L''=2''P'', ''H''<sup>3</sup>''L''<sup>2</sup>=4''P'', ''H''<sup>2</sup>''L''<sup>3</sup>=4''P'', ''H''<sup>1</sup>''L''<sup>4</sup>=2''P'', ''L''<sup>5</sup>=1''P''. So we have (6''H''−2''E'')<sup>5</sup> = (2''H''+2''L'')<sup>5</sup> = 3264''P''.

Fulton & MacPherson gave a precise description of exactly what "general position" means (although their two propositions about this are not quite right, and are corrected in a note on page 29 of their paper).<ref>{{citation |last=Fulton |first=William |title=Algebraic geometry (Proc. Sympos., Univ. Tromsø, Tromsø, 1977) |volume=687 |pages=1–30 |year=1978 |series=Lecture Notes in Math. |chapter=Defining algebraic intersections |place=Berlin |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/BFb0062926 |isbn=978-3-540-08954-4 |mr=0527228 |last2=MacPherson |first2=Robert}}</ref> If the five conics have the properties that 
*there is no line such that every one of the 5 conics is either tangent to it or passes through one of two fixed points on it (otherwise there is a "double line with 2 marked points" tangent to all 5 conics)
*no three of the conics pass through any point (otherwise there is a "double line with 2 marked points" tangent to all 5 conics passing through this triple intersection point)
*no two of the conics are tangent 
*no three of the five conics are tangent to a line
*a pair of lines each tangent to two of the conics do not intersect on the fifth conic (otherwise this pair is a [[degenerate conic]] tangent to all 5 conics)
then the total number of conics ''C'' tangent to all 5 (counted with multiplicities) is 3264. Here the multiplicity is given by the product over all 5 conics ''C''<sub>''i''</sub> of (4 − number of intersection points of ''C'' and ''C''<sub>''i''</sub>). In particular if ''C'' intersects each of the five conics in exactly 3 points (one double point of tangency and two others) then the multiplicity is 1, and if this condition always holds then there are exactly 3264 conics tangent to the 5 given conics.

Over other algebraically closed fields the answer is similar, unless the field has [[characteristic 2]] in which case the number of conics is 51 rather than 3264.
